settings.editor: What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Arches that flatten when you stand
  • Aching in the arch, heel or inside of the ankle after activity
  • Shoes wearing unevenly on the inside edge
  • Tired legs after standing rather than sharp pain

A low arch is a shape, not automatically a problem. It matters when the way the foot rolls through stance puts strain on tissue further up — the arch, the knee, or the hip. That is the difference between flat feet that need treating and flat feet that do not.

image.alt: A podiatrist assessing the arch of a patient’s foot

settings.editor: <figcaption>A podiatrist assessing the arch of a patient’s foot</figcaption>
In detail
A flat or rolled-in foot is called over-pronation. Some rolling in is normal: it is how the foot absorbs shock. The problem is when it goes too far for too long.

image.alt: Heels rolling in before an orthotic and upright after it

settings.editor: How far should a foot roll in?
Heel upright
Standing relaxed, the heel sits between upright and a few degrees tilted: 0–4°.
Up to 4°
When walking, the foot should only roll in about 4° from its neutral position to absorb impact.
Beyond that
The arch drops, the foot lengthens and the strain moves up the leg.
01
The foot is the body’s foundation: when it collapses, it brings everything above with it. A common pattern is inner heel pain in the morning, inner shin pain and inner knee pain together.
02
These biomechanical traits are often inherited and passed down through generations, often alongside a twist in the shin (pigeon-toed or out-toed).
03
A support that flattens like a pancake under thumb pressure is not supporting much. An orthotic should also sit stable on a flat surface without wobbling.
04
How firm the orthotic needs to be depends on how far your foot rolls in and on your body weight. Different shoes may need different styles.
How we diagnose it
Flat Feet is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess whether your arch position is actually causing the symptoms you have come in with.
02
If it is, we identify what is happening through stance and show you what we found.
03
Where treatment is needed it is aimed at how the foot loads, not at forcing an arch shape.

Questions

settings.title: Do flat feet always need treating?

settings.editor: No. Plenty of people have low arches and no pain. Treatment is for what the assessment finds, not for the shape itself.

settings.title: Will my child grow out of it?

settings.editor: Often, yes. Arches develop through childhood. The assessment tells you whether yours is developing as expected.
Only if the assessment shows they will change something. They are not automatic.

settings.title: Can flat feet cause knee pain?

settings.editor: They can, where the way the foot rolls changes the load at the knee. That is one of the things the assessment looks at.
No. You can book directly.

settings.editor: What it is
There are 26 bones in the foot and each joint between them has a range it should move through. Mobilisation is hands-on work to restore movement where a joint has become restricted.
People whose assessment shows a joint is not moving as it should, and that the restriction is changing how load passes through the foot.
Where it is available

image.alt: A podiatrist mobilising a patient’s foot by hand

settings.editor: In detail
The foot has 26 bones and two sesamoids. Joints can become stiff or partly dislocated (subluxed), which limits how well the foot moves.

image.alt: A practitioner mobilising the joints of a foot

settings.editor: 01
Cuboid syndrome: a bone on the outer side of the foot partly dislocates, often after an ankle sprain or with a foot that rolls in too far.
02

• Increase how far the joint moves
  • Reduce joint swelling
  • Restore normal muscle tone
  • Stretch tight tissue and break down adhesions
03
Mobilisation works through the foot, ankle, knee and hip joints. It is best used alongside orthotics and exercises.
04
Past fractures or stress fractures, a history of blood clots (DVT), fresh sprains and inflammation, severe osteoporosis or infection. Your podiatrist checks these first.
How it works here
Foot Mobilisation is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
The assessment establishes which joints are restricted and whether that restriction is relevant to your pain.
02
The joint is mobilised by hand, working through its range rather than forcing it.
03
Mobilisation is usually paired with exercises or orthotic therapy so the range gained is kept.

Questions

settings.title: Is foot mobilisation the same as a massage?

settings.editor: No. Massage works on soft tissue. Mobilisation works on the joints themselves and is directed at specific restrictions the assessment found.
It should not. The joint is worked through its range rather than forced. Tell your podiatrist if anything is uncomfortable.

settings.title: How many sessions will I need?

settings.editor: That depends on what the assessment found and how long the restriction has been there. Your podiatrist will tell you before you commit.

settings.title: Will I need exercises at home?

settings.editor: Usually. Range gained in the clinic is easier to keep if it is loaded between appointments.
No. You can book directly. If you are on a Medicare care plan your GP will refer you, and we can bill that.

settings.editor: What it is
Strapping applies tape to change how load passes through the foot, taking it off the tissue that is painful while that tissue settles.

People who need support straight away, and people for whom strapping is a test: if taping the foot a certain way relieves the pain, that tells us something useful about what an orthotic would need to do.
Where it is available

image.alt: Therapeutic strapping being applied to a patient’s foot

settings.editor: In detail
Strapping stimulates the nerve endings in the skin that sense pressure and position, improving how the body senses and controls the foot.

image.alt: Strapping tape applied around the foot and ankle

settings.editor: Four strapping techniques
Arch and heel
A figure-8 under the foot for plantar fasciitis, heel spurs and Sever’s disease.
Ankle
Supports ankle stability.
Knee
For knee pain around the kneecap.
Teenage knee
For pain at the growth area below the kneecap.
01
Strapping can protect against injury or give short-term support while other treatment takes effect.
02
How your foot responds to strapping helps show how much correction an orthotic will need.
03
For a foot that rolls in, the tape starts on the outer side to pull against it. For a foot that rolls out, it starts on the inner side.
How it works here
Foot Strapping is prescribed against a diagnosis, never against a symptom. That is what the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment is for.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
The assessment establishes which tissue is overloaded and which direction needs supporting.
02
Tape is applied to offload that tissue. You will usually know within a day or two whether it has helped.
03
Strapping is short-term by design. Where it works, it often points towards orthotic therapy as the longer-term answer.

settings.title: How long does strapping stay on?

settings.editor: What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• A feeling of standing on a pebble or a fold in your sock
  • Burning or tingling that runs into the toes
  • Numbness in the toes
  • Relief when you take your shoe off and rub the foot
  • Worse in narrow or firm-soled shoes

The forefoot takes the highest pressure of any part of the foot at push-off. Pain there usually means pressure is concentrating where it should be spread — through foot alignment, footwear width, or the way load moves across the ball of the foot.

image.alt: Diagram of Morton’s neuroma between the metatarsals

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of Morton’s neuroma between the metatarsals</figcaption>
In detail
Pain in the ball of the foot falls into two main types. They feel different and have different causes.

image.alt: Diagram of metatarsalgia, pain across the ball of the foot

settings.editor: Two main types
General, burning
Pain spread across the ball of the foot. As a rolled-in foot lengthens, it creates shearing forces on the long bones’ heads and loses the arch across the forefoot.
Localised, nerve
A swelling of the nerve that runs between the metatarsals, the long bones of the foot — usually between the 2nd/3rd or 3rd/4th toes.
01

settings.title: How a neuroma changes over time

settings.editor: It starts as localised pain, then numbness, tingling or pins and needles into the toes. Over time the body forms scar tissue around the nerve to protect it.
02

settings.title: Why it needs a proper look

settings.editor: A cyst between the toes, bursitis or a torn plantar plate can feel similar. Telling them apart is part of the assessment.
03
Orthotics with a metatarsal dome, which supports the arch across the forefoot, dry needling, foot mobilisation and massage.
How we diagnose it
Forefoot Pain is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess where pressure is concentrating across the forefoot as you walk.
02
We work out whether the problem is mechanical, footwear, or both, and explain what we found.
03
Treatment is aimed at redistributing that pressure rather than only settling the symptom.

settings.title: Growing Pains, Pigeon Toe and Flat Feet: When to Get Your Child Assessed

settings.editor: Many things that look worrying in a child’s feet settle on their own. The signs that mean it is worth having them assessed, and what to check in a school shoe.
DA Dr. Abbie Clinics clinical team 5 August 2026 · 4 min read
Book a session (opens online booking in a new tab) Call (02) 9545 4378

• Children’s feet and legs are still developing, and many differences in the way they walk settle with growth.
  • In-toeing, out-toeing and flexible flat feet are common in young children and often need monitoring rather than treatment.
  • Pain that limits activity, a limp, one side behaving differently, or things getting worse rather than better are reasons to book.
  • A good school shoe bends at the toes, is firm along its length, and has a straight, supportive heel.

Parents notice things. A child whose feet turn in when they run, who trips more than their friends, or who complains that their legs ache at night. Some of these settle on their own as a child grows. Some do not. The difficulty is telling which is which, and that is what an assessment is for.

A child’s foot is not a small adult foot. The bones, the arch and the rotation of the legs all change through childhood, and what is typical at three can look quite different from what is typical at eight. That is why the same observation can be entirely expected in one child and worth addressing in another.

Pigeon toe describes feet that point inwards when a child walks or runs. The rotation can come from the foot, the shin or the hip, and which one matters, because they behave differently as a child grows. Many children grow out of it.

It is worth having it assessed if it is getting more noticeable rather than less, if it is much more obvious on one side, if your child is tripping frequently, or if they are complaining of pain or tiring quickly.

Out-toeing is the reverse: feet that turn outwards, sometimes with a waddling look to the walk. Like in-toeing, some out-toeing is expected at particular ages and resolves with growth, and it is assessed in the same way.

Young children often look flat-footed, and arches typically develop through childhood. A foot that looks flat when standing but shows an arch when the child stands on tiptoe is often described as flexible, and in many children needs nothing more than monitoring.

Flat feet are worth assessing when they come with pain, when the foot seems stiff, when one foot is noticeably different from the other, or when a child is avoiding activity because their feet or legs hurt.

Many children go through periods of aching legs, usually in the evening or at night, often after an active day, and typically in both legs rather than one spot. These episodes are common and usually settle.

Leg pain in an active child can also come from how the feet and legs are loading during sport, including pain around the heel or just below the kneecap, where growth plates can become irritated. That kind of pain tends to relate to activity and sit in a particular place, and it is worth having looked at.

settings.title: Signs it is time to book

settings.editor:
• pain that stops your child doing things they enjoy, or that they are avoiding sport because of it
  • a limp, or one leg or foot behaving differently from the other
  • tripping or falling noticeably more than other children their age
  • pain that sits in one specific spot, or happens during the day as well as at night
  • something that is getting worse over months rather than better
  • shoes that wear out very unevenly or quickly

• there is swelling, redness or warmth around a joint, or your child has a fever
  • they have a limp that has not settled within a few days, or will not put weight on a leg
  • pain repeatedly wakes them from sleep in the same place
  • the pain followed a fall or injury

A children’s podiatry assessment looks at how your child stands, walks and runs, and compares that against what is expected for their age. We explain what we found in plain terms, including when the answer is that nothing needs doing yet. Where something does, treatment is staged around growth and reviewed as they develop.
Children are seen at all of our clinics. Bring the shoes your child wears most, including school shoes.

settings.title: What to check in a school shoe

settings.editor: Children spend a large part of the week in their school shoes, so they are worth choosing carefully. Three quick checks you can do in the shop:

image.alt: Illustration: a shoe should bend only at the toe box, should not have cut-outs in the arch area, and should not collapse in the arch
Illustration: the length of a shoe should be firm, the heel should not collapse, and the shoe should not twist from side to side
Illustration: the heel seam should be straight and centred, and the heel counter firm enough not to collapse under mild thumb pressure

settings.editor: This article is general information, not a diagnosis. Everyone’s situation is different, so if you have pain or a concern about your feet or legs, have it assessed by a health professional.

settings.editor: What you notice
If this sounds like your pain, there is a structural reason for it. The assessment is what finds it.

• Sharp pain under the heel with the first steps out of bed
  • Pain that eases as you warm up, then returns after sitting
  • Tenderness when you press the inside of the heel
  • Worse after a long day standing, or after exercise rather than during it

Most heel pain comes from pronation — the foot rolling in too far. As the arch drops, the foot lengthens and the plantar fascia is elongated, and that repeated stretching causes micro-tears at the base of the heel, where the fascia attaches. A heel spur seen on an X-ray is frequently a result of that loading rather than the cause of the pain.

image.alt: Diagram of a heel spur and the calcaneal attachment of the plantar fascia

settings.editor: <figcaption>Diagram of a heel spur and the calcaneal attachment of the plantar fascia</figcaption>
In detail
Most heel pain comes from the thick band of tissue under the foot (the plantar fascia) pulling where it attaches to the heel bone. Where on the heel it hurts is a clue to how your foot is moving.

image.alt: A hand holding a painful heel

settings.editor: Where it hurts points to why
Foot rolls in
Linked with the foot rolling inwards too far (over-pronation), which stretches the inner edge of the fascia.
Rolls out, then in
The foot lands on its outer edge, then rolls in. The heel becomes a pivot point for both movements.
Foot rolls out
Linked with the foot rolling outwards (supination), loading the outer attachment.
01

settings.title: Why the first steps hurt most

settings.editor: People often describe it as a hot, sharp pain through the heel when they get out of bed, taking 5–10 minutes to ease. It returns after sitting, and burns after a long day standing.
02

• Plantar fasciitis: repeated strain causes tiny tears and inflammation at the attachment.
  • Plantarfasciosis: over time the tissue thickens and scars, often without inflammation. It can be seen on ultrasound and is harder to treat the longer it is left.
  • Heel spur: a bony growth that forms as the body compensates. The pain feels the same.
03

Two people can both be told they have plantar fasciitis for opposite reasons: one whose longer leg rolls in to level up with the shorter one, another whose foot rolls out. The treatment is different for each, which is why the assessment comes first.
04
Orthotics with additions, strapping, massage and foot adjustments, shockwave, dry needling and injection therapy, each aimed at the area that hurts.
How we diagnose it
Heel Pain is diagnosed with the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment, so treatment is prescribed against a finding rather than a symptom.

image.alt: Dr Abbie Najjarine assessing a patient’s gait on a treadmill

settings.editor: 01
We assess how you stand, walk and load rather than only pressing the sore spot, because the heel is usually where the pain shows up and not where it starts.
02
We identify what is overloading the tissue — alignment, footwear, activity, or the way the leg above the foot is working — and explain what we found.
03
Treatment is then prescribed against that finding, which is why two people with the same heel pain can leave with different plans.

Questions

settings.title: Why does my heel hurt most first thing in the morning?

settings.editor: The tissue under the heel shortens overnight and is loaded suddenly when you stand. That first-step pain is one of the most recognisable features of the problem and is part of what the assessment asks about.

settings.title: Is a heel spur causing my pain?

settings.editor: Often not. Spurs show up on X-rays of people with no pain at all, and plenty of people with heel pain have no spur. The assessment looks at loading rather than at the spur alone.

settings.title: How long does heel pain take to settle?

settings.editor: That depends on how long it has been there and what is causing it. Your podiatrist will give you a realistic timeframe at the assessment rather than a standard answer.
Rest alone often helps while you are resting and returns when you go back to normal, because it does not change what caused the overload. That cause is what the assessment is aimed at.

Common questions

settings.title: Do I need a referral to see a podiatrist?

settings.editor: No. Podiatry is a primary contact profession in Australia, so you can book directly. If you are on a Medicare care plan your GP will refer you, and we can bill that.

settings.title: What happens at a biomechanical assessment?

settings.editor: We assess how you stand, walk and load, identify the structure causing the pain, and explain what we found before any treatment starts. That is the Najjarine Biomechanical Assessment. Allow about 45 minutes for a first appointment.

settings.title: How much does an appointment cost?

settings.editor: Fees vary by appointment type and by clinic. Call the clinic you want to attend and reception will quote you before you book.

settings.title: Can I claim on the day?

settings.editor: Yes. We have HICAPS at every clinic, so private health rebates come off on the spot. Medicare care plans and NDIS plans are accepted.
